(Simon Jones/Pool Photo via AP) (Simon Jones/Simon Jones/Pool The Sun via AP) By JILL LAWLESS, Associated Press July 27, 2026 at 2:11 pm EDT LONDON — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and new U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham met Monday at a British naval base and discussed joint drone projects and Ukraine's urgent need for ballistic missile interceptors to counter Russian attacks. Zelenskyy's visit was the first by a foreign leader since Burnham took office a week ago, and the prime minister said it signaled the U.K.'s "unwavering" support for Kyiv to defend itself against Russia's 4-year-old, full-scale invasion. His predecessor, Keir Starmer , was in the Ukrainian capital less than two weeks ago in his last overseas trip before leaving office, and Burnham said he planned to visit soon. Burnham is the fifth British prime minister Zelenskyy has dealt with since Russia launched the war in 2022. "You are the first leader I have welcomed in person since taking office, and that is no accident,” Burnham told Zelenskyy. “It is intended to send a very clear message: we are with Ukraine 100%, I am personally with you 100%, and I will honor every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full.” Zelenskyy said the two countries' relationship was “stronger than ever.” The meeting, aboard the aircraft carrier HMS Queen Elizabeth docked at Portsmouth on England’s south coast, came a day before Zelenskyy is expected to visit U.S. President Donald Trump in Washington. Burnham said they had “talked at length” about Kyiv's need for more interceptors to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles, “particularly in terms of Ukraine protecting critical national infrastructure during the winters.” “We’ve taken away some things that we will now follow up with our partners,” Burnham said after the meeting. Russia has intensified strikes on gas stations, power facilities and other infrastructure this year in a broad campaign to strain Ukraine’s logistics and energy networks. Zelenskyy said on X that the leaders also discussed “joint defense production.” Britain and Ukraine already have a deal to work together on new drones, and Zelenskyy told Sky News beforehand that he hoped to build a “big, big factory” in Britain. They also met more than 200 Ukrainian military personnel who have spent three weeks in Britain for an exercise aimed at strengthening their fighting capabilities and measures to counter mines in the Black Sea, the U.K. government said. Burnham announced that the U.K. will give Ukraine the intellectual property behind its new “Stone Cloak” electronic warfare system, which is capable of jamming Russian air defenses to stop drones from being detected. Ukraine has expanded its campaign of frequent drone attacks deep inside Russia that have targeted oil facilities, military factories and, most recently, logistical centers, bringing the war home to millions of Russians and raising pressure on President Vladimir Putin . The raids have shattered Putin’s narrative of the conflict as something that doesn’t affect the lives of ordinary people in his country. But he has remained undeterred and Russia has ramped up its aerial campaign, regularly bombarding Ukraine with missiles and drones. Russia and Ukraine trade drone attacks Russia again attacked Ukraine overnight with 147 long-range drones, according to Ukraine's air force, which said it intercepted or jammed 123 of them. In Zaporizhzhia, one person was killed and two injured in attacks on the city that damaged a residential high-rise and several private homes overnight, according to regional administration head Ivan Fedorov. A Russian strike on the town of Balakliia in the Kharkiv region killed one person and wounded eight, according to Vitalii Karabanov, head of the city military administration. In the Nikopol district of the Dnipropetrovsk region, Russian strikes damaged a kindergarten, residential buildings and infrastructure, injuring a woman and a 6-year-old boy, according to administration head Oleksandr Hanzha. In the eastern Kharkiv region, regional council member Oleksandr Skoryk said Russian forces destroyed every gas station along the highway between Kharkiv and Poltava, a distance of about 150 kilometers (93 miles). The highway is a key supply route linking Kharkiv, the country’s second-largest city and a regional hub close to the Russian border, with central Ukraine. Romania’s Ministry of National Defense said a drone briefly entered its airspace before crossing the river border into Ukraine, where explosions were subsequently reported. It said two F-16 fighter jets were deployed to monitor airspace. The drone’s incursion into Romanian airspace marked the fourth such incident in as many days. The three previous drones were all shot down by the NATO member. In Moscow, Russia’s Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 276 Ukrainian drones overnight. Rostov regional Gov. Yuri Slyusar said five people, including a child, were killed when a Ukrainian drone hit an apartment building in Rostov-on-Don. Ukraine’s military General Staff said Ukrainian forces struck an export terminal in Rostov-on-Don, setting it ablaze. The Ukrainian military said other strikes in the Moscow-held part of the Kherson region targeted a ground relay station used to control drones and a bridge over the Henichesk Strait that Russia uses for military logistics. Russian fuel and supply depots were also hit. In the city of Belgorod in southwestern Russia near the border with Ukraine, a Ukrainian drone attack injured 12, including two children, according to regional emergency officials. Iran vows retaliation after Ukrainian attack on a ship Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Ukraine struck an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea, killing a sailor. In a statement on X on Sunday, Araghchi denounced the attack as a “blatant U.N. Charter violation done at Israel’s behest to drag Europe into its war.” He said he made it clear in calls with the European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov that the attack “can't go unanswered.” Zelenskyy said on X that Ukrainian long-range strikes in the Caspian Sea over the weekend achieved “very good results,” adding the targets included “vessels involved in transporting military cargo linked to Iran, as well as a warship.” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha rejected Iran’s threats of retaliation as unjustified and groundless, saying Tehran's weapons supplies to Russia have made it a direct accomplice to Moscow's aggression. “Iran has no standing to pretend to be a victim,” he posted on X, and called its references to the U.N. Charter “absurd.” Sybiha said Iran’s statements were an attempt to divert attention from Russia’s attacks on civilian shipping in the Black Sea, which would be a focus of an emergency U.N. Security Council meeting Monday. ___ Hanna Arhirova and Illia Novikov in Kyiv, Ukraine, and Stephen McGrath in Bucharest, Romania, contributed. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. https://telex.hu/g7/penz/2026/08/14/ener.text: Menü Kereső Úgy sikerült összerakni a hazai energiarendszert, hogy „az egész régió Magyarországból él” Pénz Legfontosabb A temelíni atomerőmű hűtőtornyai Dél-Csehországban, 2026. augusztus 7-én – Fotó: Martin Divisek / MTI / EPA Jandó Zoltán A magyar energiarendszer rengeteg hibájára rávilágított a mostani válság. Eddig elsősorban az ellátási kérdések és a hiányzó kapacitás volt a fókuszban, de a dolognak van egy elég súlyos anyagi oldala is. Az elmúlt évek átgondolatlan fejlesztésein évente százmilliárdokat bukik az ország, miközben az egészségesebb energiamixszel bíró régiós országok és kereskedőik rengeteget kereshetnek a magyar rendszer hibáin. A cechet végső soron a hazai vállalatok fizetik meg, ez pedig a teljes nemzetgazdaságnak rossz. A nyári modell Múlt héten részletes cikkben mutattuk meg , hogy honnan érkezik az áram Magyarországra azokban az órákban, amikor a paksi atomerőmű kiesése miatt erősen visszafogott termelés az áramigénynek csak töredékét képes fedezni. Az egyik fontos megállapítás az volt, hogy elvileg lenne hazai gáz- és szénalapú erőművi kapacitás, amely átvehetné a paksi termelés nagy részét, mégsem ez történt. Az itthoni erőművek a Paks miatt hiányzó mennyiség alig negyedét-ötödét vették át, a többit importból fedeztük. Ennek pedig egyszerűen piaci okai voltak: a hazai termelés drágább lett volna, mint külföldről villamos energiát behozni. A cikk másik fontos megállapítása pedig az volt, hogy bár az import jelentős hányada Szlovákia felől érkezett az országba, ám ennek az áramnak a zöme valójában nem északi szomszédunktól származott, rajtuk is csak keresztülfolyt. A hazai többletigényt kiszolgáló villamos energia nagy része minden jel szerint Csehországból érkezett. A cseh termelés és export a nap során végig elég szépen lekövette a magyar keresletet. Nem fedezte ugyan a teljes itteni hiányt, de elég jelentős részét igen. Ezt a fenti ábrával szemléltettük. A grafikon azt mutatja meg, hogy augusztus első napjaiban a cseh áramtermelés és -kivitel akkor pörgött fel, amikor a magyar import is. Ám ami ennél is érdekesebb, hogy ez egyáltalán nem egyedi eset. Nyáron lényegében végig ez a modell. A lenti ábra június második felében mutatja meg minden napra negyedórás bontásban a hazai és cseh export-import szaldót (tehát a behozatal és kivitel aktuális különbségét), illetve a csehországi termelést. Jól látszik, hogy a folyamatok szinte mindennap nagyon hasonlók: a magyar és a cseh külkereskedelem egymás inverzeként alakul, miközben a cseh többlettermelés a magyar keresletet követi. A mostani helyzethez képest annyi a nem jelentéktelen különbség, hogy június második felében működött a paksi atomerőmű. Azért is választottuk ezt az időszakot, mert ebben a bő két hétben szinte végig teljes kapacitáson termelt Paks. Csak június legvégén kellett visszaterhelni az erőművet a hőség miatt, ám akkor is csak szűk negyedével csökkent az előállított villamos energia mennyisége. Olcsón adunk, drágán veszünk Összességében tehát az látszik, hogy ha nagyjából normálisan üzemel a paksi atomerőmű, akkor napközben – amikor termelnek a hazai napelemek – a magyar piacon túlkínálat van, azaz sokkal több az áram, mint amennyit elhasználnánk, ezért ilyenkor exportálunk. Naplemente után aztán hirtelen visszaesik a termelés, és ezzel párhuzamosan megugrik a fogyasztás, így ebben az időszakban jelentős importra szorulunk. A cseh export és termelés pedig általában pont fordítva alakul. Náluk napközben esik vissza az export, vagy fordul át egyenesen importba, és az esti órákban pörög fel a kivitel. A két ország áramkereskedelme közötti különbség igazából akkor nyer értelmet, ha a korábbi ábrán a termelési, illetve export-import adatok mellett feltüntetjük az áramár napon belüli alakulását is. Ezt mutatja a fenti grafikon, amiről így már könnyen leolvasható, hogy míg Magyarországról akkor exportálnak villamos energiát, amikor az áram ára rendkívül alacsony, extrém esetben nulla vagy akár negatív, és akkor importálnak, amikor nagyon magas, addig a cseheknél épp fordítva. Ott akkor nő az import, amikor olcsón lehet vásárolni, és akkor ugrik meg a kivitel, amikor drágán lehet eladni. Valószínűleg nem kell sokat magyarázni, hogy melyik modell az egészségesebb. Olcsón venni és drágán adni általában üzletileg előnyösebb, mint fordítva. Ennek megfelelően egy átlagos napon a cseh szereplőknél jelentős nyereség, a magyaroknál pedig komoly veszteség keletkezik amiatt, hogy mikor tudják értékesíteni az áramot. Június második felében a negyedórás árakkal számolva a cseh nettó export napi 4 millió euró, azaz 1,4 milliárd forint körüli többletet mutatott, míg itthon 2,5 millió euró, azaz 900 millió forint volt a hiány. Azaz Magyarországon aktuális áron számolva naponta 900 millió forinttal többet fizettünk az áramimportért, mint amennyit az exportért kaptunk. Eddig elsősorban országokról beszéltünk, de ennek csak az az oka, hogy külkereskedelmi és termelési adatok is elsősorban nemzeti szinten érhetők el. A villamosenergia-piacon azonban nem országok kereskednek egymással, hanem fogyasztók, termelők és az őket összekapcsoló energiakereskedők. Illetve természetesen szabályozói és finanszírozói oldalról egyes esetekben megjelenik az állam vagy valamilyen állami szereplő is. Ez azért fontos, mert emiatt a rosszul vagy jól kialakított energiamix nyeresége és vesztesége sem (elsősorban) az állami költségvetésekben csapódik le, hanem a különböző piaci szereplőknél. Nyertesek és vesztesek Csehországban a legnagyobb nyertesek valószínűleg azok a szereplők, amelyek képesek eltárolni a napközben olcsón megvett áramot, és eladni azt jóval magasabb áron az esti órákban. A múlt heti cikkünkben is jeleztük, hogy amikor este felpörög a cseh export, akkor ebben jelentős szerepük van a szivattyús tározós erőműveknek. Az ilyen létesítmények úgy működnek, hogy azokban az időszakokban, amikor olcsó a villamos energia, áramot felhasználva vizet szivattyúznak egy alacsonyabban fekvő tározóból egy magasabban fekvőbe. Később, amikor felmennek az árak, akkor a vizet leengedik, közben villamos energiát termelve. A cseheknél viszonylag sok ilyen erőmű van. Ahogy a fenti ábrán is látszik, augusztus első napjaiban az esti órákban a teljes termelés akár tizedét is ilyenek adták. Ezzel pedig egész biztosan jelentős jövedelemre tettek szert. Illetve tett szert a CEZ cseh energetikai óriás, hiszen a legtöbb ilyen létesítményt ez a – 70 százalékban állami tulajdonban lévő – vállalat üzemelteti . Jelenleg hármat, de épp a közelmúltban jelentették be, hogy 2033-ig kialakítanak még egy szivattyús tározós erőművet. A cseheknél tehát elég jól be lehet lőni, hogy vélhetően melyik piaci szereplő a legnagyobb nyertes. Itthon ez már nem feltétlenül ennyire egyértelmű. Magyarországon azok a szereplők veszítenek a rosszul időzített exporton és importon, amelyek – tárolókapacitás híján – kénytelenek napközben olcsón eladni az általuk megtermelt áramot, illetve amelyek a nap végén csak drágán tudnak vásárolni. Mivel a lakossági áram ára fix, ezért az esti drága áram csak a vállalati fogyasztókat sújtja. A hazai cégek emiatt nemzetközi összevetésben is magas áramárral szembesülnek. Az olcsó értékesítés, illetve export alapesetben a termelők problémája lenne, a rendszer működése miatt azonban valójában ők a legtöbbször köszönik szépen, jól vannak. Abban az időszakban ugyanis, amikor túltermelés van az országban, és így olcsón exportálunk, az áram nagy részét a napelemek állítják elő. Márpedig az ilyen parkok létesítését úgy ösztönözte az állam az elmúlt években, hogy a piaci árnál jóval magasabb átvételi árat biztosított számukra. Magyarul a napelemes erőművek üzemeltetői nem a rendkívül alacsony piaci áron értékesítik az általuk megtermelt villamos energiát, hanem jóval drágábban. Korábban az állam egy fix díjat határozott meg, amit a piaci ártól függetlenül megkaptak a termelők (ez volt a kötelező átvételi rendszer, azaz a KÁT), később pedig piaci ár feletti prémiumot adott (ez a megújuló támogatási rendszer azaz a METÁR). A lényeg azonban, hogy az alacsony árú exporton nem a termelők buknak, hiszen az állam – azon belül egészen pontosan a hazai villamosenergia-hálózat működéséért felelős rendszerirányító, a Mavir – jelentős összegeket fizet számukra, hogy kompenzálja az alacsony árakat. Elvileg tehát az államnál csapódik le a veszteség, ám ez sem ilyen egyszerű. A Mavir ugyanis nem saját forrásból fedezi a kifizetéseket, hanem a kereskedőkre tolja, amelyek aztán szétporlasztják ezt a felhasználók között. Természetesen itt is csak a vállalati vevők jöhetnek szóba, hiszen a lakossági fogyasztók rezsicsökkentett fix áron kapják a villamos energiát, abba a tarifába pedig az elmúlt években semmit nem lehetett beépíteni. Pedig tényleg hatalmas összegről van szó. A Mavir saját adatai szerint a nyári hónapokban csak a KÁT-kifizetés több tízmilliárd forint, de a jóval kisebb termelés ellenére még télen is milliárdos nagyságrendű. A legutóbbi adatközlés szerint az idei első fél évben a teljes kifizetés meghaladta a százmilliárd forintot. Összességében tehát a rosszul összeállított hazai energiamix vesztesei a vállalatok. A drága esti áram és a napelemes termelőknek fizetett kompenzáció is végső soron a cégek számláját növeli. Ennek azonban nyilván vannak tovagyűrűző hatásai. A költségeket a vállalatok áthárítják a fogyasztókra, ami növeli az áraikat (és így az inflációt). Emiatt viszont a magyar cégek termékei drágábbak lesznek, ami rontja a versenyképességüket és így a teljes gazdaság teljesítményét is. Meg lehetett volna előzni A legrosszabb az egészben, hogy mindezt az elmúlt évek-évtizedek rosszul átgondolt hazai energiafejlesztései okozták, és nem is lett volna olyan nehéz elkerülni. A fő probléma a nappali órákra koncentrált napelemes termelés, illetve az, hogy az ekkor előállított villamos energiát nem tudják a piaci szereplők eltárolni. „A világ más pontjain a 2020-as évek elejétől hirdettek meg úgy pályázatokat nap- és szélenergiás rendszerek telepítésére, hogy a kiírásban már kötelező elemként szerepelt kapcsolódó tárolókapacitás kiépítése is” – mondta a G7-nek Perger András, az Energiaklub szakértője. Nálunk azonban nagyon későn kapcsolt a szabályozó, így a napelemek teljesítményéhez képest arányaiban rendkívül kevés a tárolói kapacitás. Pedig az akkumulátorárak alakulása és a napon belüli hatalmas áramáringadozás miatt ezek már elég régóta piaci alapon is simán megtérülő beruházások lennének. Csakhogy a napelemparkok tulajdonosai a támogatási rendszer miatt nagyon sokáig egyáltalán nem voltak rákényszerítve, hogy tárolásban is gondolkodjanak, hiszen így is, úgy is megkapják az állam által garantált árat vagy prémiumot az általuk termelt energiáért. Múlt heti hírlevelünkben mutattuk be azokat az adatokat , amelyekből kiderül, hogy Magyarországon volt az egyik legalacsonyabb az energiatárolós kapacitások aránya a napelemesekhez képest tavaly abban a 21 európai uniós tagállamban, amelyre vonatkozóan rendelkezésre állnak a 2025-ös adatok. Itthon 8,3 gigawattnyi napelem mellett 110 megawattnyi energiatároló volt, ami az egyik legrosszabb arány az EU-ban. Bár az idén felgyorsult az akkumulátorok telepítése, a lemaradásunk még így is hatalmas. Szakértők szerint a jelenlegi kapacitás alsó hangon három-négyszeresére lenne szükség. Ha már jelenleg is ennyi akkumulátor lenne az országban, akkor nagyon jelentősen csökkenne az áramár napközbeni ingadozása, és így a rosszul ütemezett exporton és importon elszenvedett veszteség. A napelemek felpörgése idején ugyanis az olcsó áramot felszívnák az akkumulátorok. A villamos energia így egyrészt az országban maradna, másrészt már nem is lenne annyira olcsó, hiszen a tárolók többletkeresletet generálnának. Az árak emelkedése ebben az időszakban azért lenne előnyös, mert csökkentené a megújulótámogatási rendszer – végső soron a hazai vállalatokat terhelő – költségeit. Ezzel párhuzamosan az esti árcsúcs idején többletkínálat formájában megjelenne a piacon a napközben eltárolt hazai áram. Ez pedig csökkentené az árakat és az importigényt is, azaz az áringadozáson elért nyereség egy része is a hazai szereplőknél csapódna le. Nem csak a csehek Bár a cikkben a cseh energiarendszert állítottuk szembe a magyarral, mivel a fizikai áramlások alapján itt a leginkább szembetűnő a különbség, de nem Csehország az egyetlen régiós állam, ahol sokkal átgondoltabban sikerült fejleszteni az energiarendszert a hazainál. Vannak például szivattyús tározós erőművek Ausztriában és Szlovákiában is, így ezekből az országokból is rendszeresen importálunk drága áramot az esti órákban. A villamos energia külkereskedelmi mérlege és áramtermelői portfóliójának összetétele pedig szinte mindenhol sokkal egészségesebb, mint nálunk. „Lényegében az egész régió Magyarországból, a magyar áramdeficit drága eladásából és a magyar napos áramexport olcsó megvásárlásából él. Ezáltal pedig a magyar költségvetésből és a magyar ipari fagyasztókból” – foglalta össze röviden a jelenlegi helyzetet Turai József, a T-Energy Advisory Ltd. szakembere. https://www.budapesttimes.hu/history/he-.text: The Budapest Times He built this city on dreams and stone: The architect behind Budapest’s age of grandeur Written by Hedvig Ujvári One hundred years ago, on 31 July 1926, Alajos Hauszmann died. Born in Buda to a family of German roots and educated, among other places, at Berlin’s Bauakademie, he shaped Budapest during the great period of urban expansion more profoundly than almost any other architect – as the designer of monumental government buildings, the architect of the Royal Palace and the famous New York Palace as well as the teacher of several generations of architects. Alajos Hauszmann was born in Buda on 9 June 1847. His family had Bavarian roots; the Hauszmanns thus belonged to the German-speaking segment of Buda’s population from which many of the city’s merchants, craftsmen and members of the urban middle class emerged in the 19th century. Hauszmann’s biography is also an example of how naturally German educational traditions, Hungarian national identity and the urban culture of the Dual Monarchy could overlap in the second half of the century. His education combined practical experience in construction with academic training from an early stage. While still a teenager, Hauszmann worked as a mason, receiving his journeyman’s certificate in 1863. Such a practical foundation was by no means unusual for architects of his generation and probably had a significant influence on his later interest in construction and materials. He subsequently studied at the Royal Joseph Polytechnic in Buda. In 1866, he went to Berlin and continued his education at the renowned Bauakademie. At the time, Berlin was one of Central Europe’s foremost intellectual centres for architecture. The Bauakademie represented the Prussian tradition of combining construction, function and historical architectural language. Hauszmann studied there for five semesters. At the same time, several other young Hungarians were also studying in Berlin, including Ödön Lechner and Gyula Pártos. The generation of Hungarian architects who would later shape Budapest therefore received at least part of their education within the same German academic environment. A tribute to Hauszmann published in 1914 retrospectively described Berlin and its Bauakademie as virtually an “oracle” for Hungarian architects of the period. Accordingly, Hauszmann’s student designs initially displayed distinctly Berlin characteristics. Yet he did not remain permanently bound to this influence. A study tour through Germany, France and Italy in 1869–70 decisively broadened his horizons. The Italian Renaissance in particular would become one of his most important sources of inspiration. This reveals an important feature of his development: Hauszmann did not simply adopt German Historicism but transformed what he had learned in Berlin. From Prussian austerity, the Italian Renaissance, later Baroque forms and eventually individual elements of Art Nouveau, he developed an architecture tailored to the representational needs of a rapidly modernising Hungary. After returning home, Hauszmann initially worked in the office of Antal Skalnitzky. As early as 1868, however, he also began his exceptionally long academic career. At the Technical University, he first worked as an assistant and later became a professor, teaching there for more than four decades in total. Today’s BME (Budapest University of Technology and Economics) regards him not only as one of the country’s most important architects but also as one of the formative figures in Hungarian architectural education. This dual role as practitioner and teacher was crucial to Hauszmann’s importance. He not only designed buildings himself but also shaped the next generation through his students. Many architects who later became prominent studied under him or worked in his office for a time. Hauszmann ran one of the major architectural practices of his era, combining academic teaching, technical expertise, public commissions and entrepreneurial organisation. His influence therefore extended far beyond the number of buildings he personally designed. At a time when Budapest was growing from a recently unified city into a European metropolis, architects were needed who could master the organisational challenges of major construction projects as effectively as their aesthetic aspects. Hauszmann embodied this new professional type almost perfectly. He also held senior positions at the university and served as rector of the Technical University at the beginning of the 20th century. In 1924, he was elected an honorary member of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences. Hauszmann’s early works were still clearly influenced by German and Italian Neo-Renaissance architecture. Before long, however, he moved away from the Berlin interpretation of Renaissance architecture and increasingly sought his models directly in Italy. This phase is characterised by rigorously articulated façades, clear proportions and comparatively restrained decoration. Typical examples include schools, technical institutes and hospitals. The secondary school on Markó Street, the buildings of the Museum of Technology and various medical institutions show Hauszmann as an architect of the modern state: the aim was not merely beauty, but the creation of new institutions for education, science, healthcare and justice. Even here, it is evident that Historicism for Hauszmann by no means amounted simply to quoting historical forms. He was interested in new structural systems and technical possibilities. In his early buildings, he experimented with iron supports and more modern ceiling structures. The façades remained historicist, but behind them was an architect who closely followed the structural changes of the industrial age. Hauszmann’s career coincided with Budapest’s spectacular development following the Austro-Hungarian Compromise of 1867 and the unification of the city in 1873. Within just a few decades, boulevards, ring roads, railway stations, ministries, banks, theatres, schools and grand apartment buildings were constructed. The capital sought not merely to grow, but visibly to claim the status of a European metropolis. Hauszmann was one of its most important architects. He designed residential and commercial buildings on Andrássy Avenue and the Grand Boulevard, urban palaces for the aristocracy as well as public institutions. His architecture thus reflected a society that expressed itself through construction: the state, the upper middle class, the financial world and the aristocracy all required representative spaces in which social and political aspirations could be translated into stone. One particularly interesting work from this period was the palace of Count Géza Batthyány on Teréz Boulevard. Contemporary observers saw it almost as a scaled-down variation of Florence’s Palazzo Strozzi. The building clearly demonstrates Hauszmann’s intensive engagement with Italian Renaissance forms. Palais Batthyány – Photo: Jan Mainka Hauszmann was by no means merely an architect of spectacular palaces. A significant part of his work consisted of functional public buildings. His works also included Saint Stephen’s Hospital on Üllői Road. Buildings such as this demonstrate his interest in contemporary institutional architecture particularly clearly. Hospitals, schools and scientific institutions were among the new architectural requirements of modern Budapest, and Hauszmann developed solutions that combined functional demands with a representative exterior. The same applies to the secondary school on Markó Street and the expansion of buildings belonging to the Technical University. Renaissance influences were even more dominant here, frequently expressed in a sober, almost disciplined form. These less spectacular works are at least as important for understanding Hauszmann as his later monumental buildings. They reveal an architect who participated in building the institutional infrastructure of a modern state. In the 1890s, Hauszmann’s architectural language changed. His buildings became more monumental, dynamic and Baroque in character. Perhaps the best-known example is the New York Palace on what is now Erzsébet Boulevard, built for the New York Life Insurance Company. The aim here was no longer the restrained elegance of a Renaissance palazzo. The building was designed to attract attention. Its richly articulated façade, sculptural ornamentation, towers, figures and Baroque-inspired forms virtually embodied the capital’s new ambitions. A contemporary tribute aptly observed that the New York Palace had been created for Budapest as a world city. Hauszmann’s talent for monumental architecture was manifested even more clearly in the Palace of Justice on what is now Kossuth Lajos Square, the building that housed the Royal Curia. Constructed between 1891 and 1896, it is one of his principal works. Its location opposite Parliament gave it particular symbolic significance from the outset. The legislature and the judiciary faced one another architecturally. Hauszmann designed a building whose monumentality arose not merely from its decoration but from the rigorous organisation of its axes, staircases, halls and courtyards. The Palace of Justice The Palace of Justice also demonstrates the extent to which Hauszmann understood Historicism as a language for expressing institutional significance. Renaissance and Baroque forms were not intended as nostalgic reconstructions of a bygone age. They were meant to convey authority, permanence and dignity. This building in particular played a major role in establishing his international reputation. Hauszmann himself regarded it as one of the most important works of his career. When Miklós Ybl died in 1891, Hauszmann took over the expansion of the Royal Palace in Buda. It became the largest and most symbolically significant commission of his career. Over roughly a decade and a half, he profoundly transformed the palace complex. Ybl had already planned extensive additions. Hauszmann, however, did not simply continue this work but substantially redesigned major parts of the ensemble. The palace was now intended to reflect both Budapest’s political position within the Dual Monarchy and the representational ambitions of the Kingdom of Hungary. The Buda Castle Hauszmann expanded the complex northwards, designed new wings and interiors, and gave the Danube-facing side its monumental, symmetrical appearance. Particularly distinctive was the enormous central dome, which from then on dominated the Buda skyline. The interiors were also conceived as a total work of art. Hauszmann collaborated with leading Hungarian painters, sculptors and craftsmen. Rooms such as Saint Stephen’s Hall combined architecture, wall decoration, ceramics, woodwork and furnishings into a representative ensemble. The palace was therefore also a cultural and political project. Deliberately Hungarian accents were incorporated into its historical vocabulary; ornamental motifs derived from folk art and references to national history were integrated into the design. Contemporary critics already noted that Hauszmann was becoming increasingly concerned with the question of what a modern Hungarian architecture might look like. The Second World War and subsequent alterations destroyed large parts of these interiors. Today’s debate surrounding Hauszmann is therefore inseparable from the palace’s lost appearance – although the current reconstruction projects deserve a separate discussion. Hauszmann is generally described as one of the great representatives of Hungarian Historicism. This is correct, but it does not tell the whole story. His work went through several phases: from the Berlin- and Italian-influenced Renaissance Historicism of his early years, through an increasingly monumental Neo-Baroque architectural language, to a more restrained late period in which Art Nouveau influences can also be identified. BME describes his development in similar terms: Renaissance forms dominated his early works, while Baroque and eventually Secessionist elements appeared later. Hauszmann was therefore less a dogmatic follower of any particular style than an architect who regarded historical forms as a flexible repertoire. For him, the nature of the commission was decisive. A hospital required a different architectural language from an insurance company headquarters, a courthouse a different one from a royal residence. This adaptability partly explains his extraordinary success. It also later exposed him to criticism. For a long time, 20th-century architectural history favoured architects who radically broke with Historicism. Within this narrative, Hauszmann appeared as a representative of a disappearing era. Only later did scholars begin to recognise more clearly how closely his work was connected to technological modernisation, urban transformation and the professional institutionalisation of architecture. For all the splendour of his buildings, it should not be overlooked that Hauszmann was also deeply engaged with construction technology. Contemporary tributes emphasise that he closely followed new building materials and structural techniques. Even in his early buildings, he used iron supports and modern construction methods. In his later monumental projects, he combined historicist façades with contemporary engineering. This combination also explains his special position at the Technical University. Hauszmann was not merely an artist who composed façades; he understood architecture as a comprehensive technical and organisational process. His education in Berlin probably had a particularly lasting influence in this respect. The Bauakademie had placed particular emphasis on combining aesthetic design with structural thinking. Even after Hauszmann moved stylistically away from his early Berlin influences, this technical discipline remained an integral part of his work. One of his final major works brought Hauszmann back to the institution where he had spent his professional life: the Technical University. The main building of today’s BME on the banks of the Danube, constructed between 1905 and 1909, is one of his most important late works. The monumental building remains historicist and Neo-Baroque in character, but already displays a calmer architectural language and, in some details, the influence of Art Nouveau. It is difficult to imagine a more symbolically appropriate late work. The former student and long-serving professor designed a main building for the very university whose architectural education he himself had helped shape. At the same time, the building represents the institutionalisation of technical education in modern Hungary. Architecture and engineering received a monumental home on the banks of the Danube, visibly demonstrating the importance that technology and science had acquired for the state. Hauszmann’s impact on Hungarian architectural history cannot be measured solely in terms of buildings. For decades, he stood at the centre of academic education. His office also functioned as a practical school. Young architects could gain experience on major projects, learn technical processes and develop expertise in dealing with clients and public authorities. Later prominent architects such as Ignác Alpár and Flóris Korb were associated with his office; Korb worked for Hauszmann for around fourteen years before establishing his own practice together with Kálmán Giergl. The importance of this workshop function should not be underestimated. By around 1900, architecture no longer existed solely as an individual art but increasingly as the complex collaborative work of large architectural offices. Hauszmann was among the architects who mastered this new professional structure at an early stage. Bos , Worthy News Europe Bureau Chief DUBLIN/KYIV/BUDAPEST ( Worthy News ) – U.S. President Donald J. Trump has urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, as Russian strikes near the Ukraine-Poland border disrupted a train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and senior European officials. “Mr. Zelensky has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump told reporters during a visit to Ireland. “Let him go after targets, but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel.” Trump argued that the shortage was linked to the Russia-Ukraine war rather than the conflict in the Middle East, where fighting involving the United States and Iran has also disrupted energy markets and pushed up oil and fuel prices. Get news worthy of your attention — delivered directly to your inbox. Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian refineries and other energy facilities in recent months, saying they help finance and sustain Moscow’s war effort. Russia, meanwhile, has intensified missile and drone attacks against Ukraine. Zelensky said Sunday that Russia had launched about 2,100 drones, nearly 1,700 guided aerial bombs and 78 missiles of various types against Ukraine during the past week. TRAIN ROUTE ATTACKED The latest Russian strikes reached areas close to NATO military alliance member Poland, with railway infrastructure on the strategically important Kyiv-Warsaw route coming under attack. Johnson and the other European representatives were evacuated after their train was halted during the Russian drone attack. British media reported that another train traveling close behind was struck, leaving several people injured. The railway has become an important route for Western leaders and diplomats traveling to Kyiv because Ukraine’s airspace remains closed to regular passenger flights. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk accused Moscow of escalating the conflict, warning that Russian military activity was moving increasingly close to Poland. “Escalation on the Russian side has now become a reality, and examples of it are coming closer and closer to our border,” he said. Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said one Russian drone struck a target in western Ukraine about one kilometer (0.6 miles) from Poland and another struck about five kilometers (3 miles) from the border. A separate drone attack reportedly hit a fuel station about two kilometers (1.2 miles) from Poland, setting two trucks ablaze. PEACE TALKS POSSIBLE The escalating attacks came as Washington sought to revive negotiations aimed at ending Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Sunday that Moscow did not rule out renewed talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States in October. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner traveled to Moscow and Kyiv earlier this month in efforts to revive negotiations. Zelensky later said they had presented several “very solid and valuable ideas.” Previous U.S.-mediated negotiations failed to produce a breakthrough after direct Russian-Ukrainian talks stalled. Zelensky has also said he would be willing to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami in December. “We have to come, we have to meet, to speak and make decisions,” the Ukrainian leader told reporters. The Kremlin rejected the proposal for a meeting in Miami, maintaining that a Putin-Zelensky encounter should take place in Moscow and saying it remained unclear whether Putin would attend the G20 summit. International US Envoy Secures Release of 25 More Prisoners in Belarus The latest deal follows a series of negotiations stretching back more than a year between U.S. envoy John Coale and Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko. Save Mark Us Preferred on Google Print Presidential envoy John Coale speaks to journalists outside the U.S. Embassy in Vilnius, Lithuania, on Sept. 11, 2025, ahead of the arrival of released prisoners from Belarus. AP Photo/Mindaugas Kulbis Victoria Friedman 9/16/2026 | Updated: 9/17/2026 0:00 X 1 Belarus freed 25 prisoners on Sept. 16 in exchange for the United States’ lifting of some sanctions, and it is possible that more prisoners will be released in the future, U.S. envoy John Coale said. Coale told Reuters that the process had been successful and that U.S. President Donald Trump was “very happy with ⁠this.” Speaking from the Lithuanian capital of Vilnius, where the former detainees were taken, Coale said that he expects to return to Minsk, Belarus, in a month to secure the freedom of “hundreds” of others, including journalists, lawyers, political activists, and human rights campaigners, who are currently incarcerated in Belarus. This latest deal follows a series of negotiations stretching back more than a year between Coale and Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, a close ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin. Coale wrote in a Sept. 16 post on X that “Trump’s commitment to direct diplomacy delivers results.” He thanked Lukashenko for taking this step, as well as those in Lithuania who supported the process. Related Stories Russian Intelligence Operatives Charged by DOJ in Connection to Terrorism, Murder-for-Hire Plots Russia Says Ukraine Using Foreign Dignitaries as Human Shields “We will continue to improve US-Belarus relations and are working to secure the release of more people in the very near future,” the U.S. envoy said. “We are not finished!” Those freed include Liudmila Chekina, who was head of the online news portal TUT.BY, which was banned in 2021. Chekina told reporters that she was “overwhelmed with emotions” after ​being released from her 12-year sentence. Others freed include journalist Andrei Aliaksandrau, who had been sentenced to 14 years in prison, and his wife, Iryna Zlobina, who was serving ‌nine years. Officials, including Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko and U.S. envoy John Coale, attend a meeting in Minsk, Belarus, on Sept. 15, 2026. Press Service of the President of the Republic of Belarus/Handout via Reuters In exchange for the releases, Coale promised Lukashenko on Sept. 15 to get U.S. banks to return tens of millions of dollars in frozen Belarusian assets. The U.S. envoy had also said earlier that the United States was lifting sanctions on paints and industrial coatings manufacturer Lakokraska, as well as the state-owned Bellesbumprom, which oversees the country’s forestry and pulp and paper industries. Previous Prisoner Releases Coale’s last round of negotiations in March had resulted in the release of 250 prisoners. They were set free in exchange for sanctions relief on the financial sector, including ‌the country’s state-owned Belinvestbank. All remaining sanctions on potash companies Agrorozkvit, Belarusian ​Potash ⁠Co., and Belaruskali were also lifted. Trump appointed Coale as his special envoy to Minsk in November, after he helped negotiate the release of prisoners from Belarus, and charged him with working on the release of more. Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko speaks to reporters after voting in presidential elections in Minsk, Belarus, on Jan. 26, 2025. Pavel Bednyakov/AP Photo “[Coale] has already successfully negotiated the release of 100 hostages, and is going for an additional 50,” Trump said in a Truth Social post back in November 2025. “I would like to thank, in advance, the Highly Respected President of Belarus, Alexander Lukashenko, for his consideration on the release of these additional people.” Trump had previously urged the Belarusian leader to release 1,400 prisoners whom the U.S. president has described as hostages. Reuters contributed to this report.
